text: His name was Alexander.
In 326 BCE, he crossed into the Punjab.
On the banks of the Jaylam River, a local king called Porus was waiting.
With something the Greeks had rarely faced, war elephants.
Keep those elephants in mind.
Alexander won, and the Greek writers tell a famous story about what came next.
How do you wish to be treated?
Like a king.
Sir, he lost.
Fair.
Keep your kingdom.
Then Alexander pushed east, to the river Bias, and there his army simply stopped.
They had marched for eight years.
The monsoon rain wouldn't stop, and they had heard what was waiting beyond the river.
The Nanda kings of Magadha, with the gigantic army, thousands of elephants, and an even
bigger treasury. The soldiers refused to go any further. Alexander, who had never lost
a battle, had to turn back. He died in Babylon three years later at 32.
But a young man in India had been watching the Greeks very carefully, and he had a teacher
with a grudge. The teacher was a sharp, ruthless Brahmin named Chanakya. He had been insulted
it at the Nanda court, and thrown out in front of everyone.
So he untied the knot of his hair, and swore he would not tie it again until the Nandas
were destroyed.
That's the oath the old story's given.
And he found exactly the weapon he needed, a young man named Chandragupta Morya.
Master, shall I bring a comb?
Not until the Nandans fall.
And how long might that be?
That depends on him.
